key_insight: Natural language’s low entropy (~1 bit/char) can be explained by a multi-scale statistical process of semantic chunking: words and phrases form hierarchical chunks that create high redundancy across scales, accounting for most of English’s information compression.
problem_solved: Explains why printed English exhibits ~80% redundancy (far below random-text entropy) by providing a first-principles statistical model that captures multi-scale structure and long-range dependencies in language.
method: Introduce a generative statistical model in which meaning-bearing units form semantic chunks at multiple scales (words, phrases, clauses), with explicit rules for chunk formation and overlap.
Derive entropy-rate predictions analytically and validate with numerical simulations and comparisons to empirical entropy estimates from corpora and modern LLM outputs.
Analyze how chunk-size distributions and inter-chunk correlations reduce per-character uncertainty, linking model parameters to observed redundancy levels.
impact: Provides a principled explanation of language redundancy that informs compression limits, evaluation benchmarks for LLMs, and architectural choices to better capture hierarchical, long-range dependencies.
visual_elements: Schematic diagram of hierarchical semantic chunking (tokens → words → phrases → clauses) showing information flow and dependencies.
Entropy vs. scale chart: per-character entropy contribution at token, word, phrase levels, with cumulative reduction to ~1 bit/char.
Bar chart comparing empirical entropy estimates (corpora, LLMs) to model predictions and random-text baseline.
Flowchart of the generative model showing chunk formation rules, parameter roles, and how they affect overall redundancy.
paper_title: Semantic Chunking and the Entropy of Natural Language
paper_authors: Weishun Zhong, Doron Sivan, Tankut Can, Mikhail Katkov, Misha Tsodyks
